newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Brazil strike and cold boost coffee prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil strike and cold boost coffee prices.

text.p: World coffee prices leapt nearly three and a half percent on Tuesday as a strike hit one of Brazil's main ports and cold weather approached the country's coffee belt and revived fears in the market of a possible frost.
Elsewhere on the commodity markets, cocoa made a technical push higher to a one-year peak in London and zinc attracted another round of heated speculative buying to reach a fresh 6-3/4 year peak.
Gold, by contrast, continued its recent slump to sink to fresh 4-1/4 year lows in a market awash with pessimism. Bullion ended the session at $333.55 versus $334.45 per ounce on Monday.

A polar air mass posing the greatest frost threat to Brazil's coffee crop so far this year threatened to pass through its major growing areas from the evening of July 5, Brazilian meteorologists forecast.

With the U.S. market closed on Friday for the Fourth of July holiday, the cold weather prompted investors to begin covering exposed short positions in case it proved damaging to crops over the weekend. But some forecasters in the United States have said that although cooler weather was expected it would not bring crop-damaging frost.

Administrative workers at the port of Santos in Brazil announced they would strike indefinitely while unions tried to seal a new collective wage agreement with port officials. The strike has partially paralysed the important commodity port.

Benchmark September robusta coffee futures hit a high of $18.60 a tonne in London before settling back to end the day up $25 at $1,822. Cocoa finished the day up $10 at $1,160 per tonne on the September contract.
A 950-tonne drop in warehouse stocks at the London Metal Exchange helped give zinc prices a boost, in addition to talk of old and poor quality metal being delivered from China to Singapore.

Only two weeks ago zinc was trading around $1,350 per tonne but a bout of supply tightness has pushed the base metal to near seven-year highs. It finished the day at $1,436 per tonne, well up from its earlier level of $1,418.

On the grain markets, soybeans fell further in Chicago after a bruising selloff on Monday. The sell-off was triggered by a U.S. Department of Agriculture report that put 1997 U.S. soybean acreage well above consensus expectations.

Crude oil firmed on follow-through buying after a recent rally on last week's announced delay in Iraqi oil exports. The country's former oil sale negotiator, Abdul Amir al-Anbari, said on Friday that oil exports may not resume until August.
Benchmark Brent crude futures ended the day up 21 cents in London at $18.72
